links.note: What dropped at that moment - a spider with its silken filmy clue. The interruption that lets the poem turn a failure into an instruction.
How many attempts the spider made to reach its home - nine brave attempts. Repeated failure that did not end the effort.
How the King reacted after counting the attempts - he cried 'Sure', thinking it would strive no more. The wrong prediction the poem sets up to overturn.
How far the spider was from its cobweb door - only a foot. Narrative detail of the final climb in the poem's argument.
Reflection writing task on a time the writer felt like giving up and learned perseverance is the key - the poem's failure-is-not-the-end message applied to the student.
What the spider does after it falls the first time - it does not give up and immediately tries again. That is 28255's message exactly.
The big lesson King Bruce learned from the spider's struggle and success - 'All honour to those who try', he conquered and why shouldn't I.
Describe the spider's efforts and the challenges it faces - the thin thread, the falls, the dizziness. Imagery that carries the poem's argument, not the bare moral.
Write the spider's thought bubble after reaching its cobweb home - 'after so many tumbles, I made it'. The try-again outcome rather than the poem's craft.
Extract on King Bruce flinging himself down in a lonely mood, a monarch whose heart was sinking - the poem's opening failure.
Extract 'Up, up it ran, not a second to stay, To utter the least complaint' - the spider fell again yet did not complain, which is the failure-is-not-the-end point.
Extract 'Its head grew steady - again it went' - recovery from the previous fall and a further half-yard gained: another attempt after failure.
Extract on the spider dropping and the King stopping his thinking to watch - the moment the poem uses to turn the King's failure into an instruction.
Activity listing what the writer could See / Listen / Smell / Taste / Touch on a visit. Placing experiences against the sense each belongs to is 28257, not 28256's account of what sensory words do.
How the author's view on making the most of our senses should make us kinder - about the value of the senses themselves, so 28256 rather than the sorting exercise 28257.
Asks for two phrases describing texture - the smooth skin of a silver birch, the rough shaggy bark of a pine. A question about descriptive sensory wording, not about sorting words into senses.
The author's advice to use your eyes as if tomorrow you would be stricken blind, and to apply it to hearing, touch, smell and taste - the five senses as 28256 defines them.
Assertion-reason comparing what touch gives her with what sight would reveal - a judgement about two senses, so 28256 rather than 28257's sorting task.
Descriptive-writing task whose model answer works through scent of pine, sound of a stream and birdsong, and the feel of the air. It is a see/hear/smell/feel description, which is what 28256 covers.
How the author finds things interesting without sight - through mere touch. A question about what a sense does for her.
How the author 'sees' the outline of a face - through her fingertips. Touch standing in for sight, which is 28256's subject.
The advice to those who can see: use your eyes as if tomorrow you would be stricken blind. About using the senses fully.
How she recognises friends without her eyes - laughter and sorrow read from the feel of their faces. Touch doing the work of sight.
MCQ on Helen's advice: presume the senses will be lost tomorrow. The senses concept, not the word-sorting one.
How she recognises people - by touching their face. A sense question, so 28256.
How Helen Keller enjoys nature without sight - the shape of a leaf, smooth bark, rough pine, a bird quivering with song. Sensory description throughout.
Her advice to those who can see, extended to listening to music, touching, smelling flowers and tasting food - all five senses, which is 28256.
The moral of the essay: appreciate and fully use our senses. Sits on the senses concept, not on 28257's sorting of particular words.
How her blindness shapes her perspective - reliance on touch heightening her attention to sensory detail.
Imagine touching a rose while blind and name two details you would notice - smooth stem, sharp thorns, layered petals. Pure sensory description.
Which sound you would miss most if deaf tomorrow, and how to appreciate it today - hearing, one of the senses 28256 names.
Why Helen holds sight to be the most delightful of the senses, with two supporting reasons - a comparison between senses, so 28256.
